input.question: The Hubble Deep Field shoes thousands of galaxies from soon after the Big Bang. How is it we see these galaxies in every direction of the sky if the universe has expanded so much? Shouldn't they all be centred near one place in the sky? (i.e. near the Big Bang)
input.ground_truth: The Big Bang was not an event which happened in a particular location. It happened everywhere at once, and "everywhere" was a lot closer together at the time. The expansion is that everywhere is becoming more distant from everywhere else, not that things are hurtling away from some central point.

Okay, let’s imagine the universe is like a big, big balloon that you can draw on. 

When you blow up the balloon, the dots you drew get farther apart, right? But no matter where you look on the balloon, all the dots are moving away from each other.

Now, the Hubble Deep Field is like taking a picture of a tiny spot on the balloon and seeing lots and lots of dots (those are the galaxies). But if you look at any other tiny spot on the balloon, you’ll see more dots, too! That’s because the universe is really, really big and everywhere you look, you see galaxies that are far away.

Even though the Big Bang happened in one place a long time ago, the universe has been growing bigger and bigger in all directions. So the galaxies are not all in one spot—they’re everywhere, like dots on a balloon that’s getting bigger and bigger. That’s why we see galaxies in every direction, not just one.
